content: The term traditional medicine refers to medical knowledge systems that have been developed over centuries within various societies, predating the advent of modern medicine. These systems encompass a wide range of practices, including herbal medicine, Ayurvedic medicine, Unani medicine, acupuncture, spinal manipulation, Siddha medicine, traditional Chinese medicine, South African Muti, Yoruba Ifá, and numerous other medical traditions from around the world. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), traditional medicine involves health practices, approaches, knowledge, and beliefs that incorporate plant-based, animal-based, and mineral-based medicines, as well as spiritual therapies, manual techniques, and exercises. These methods may be applied individually or in combination to diagnose, treat, and prevent illnesses or to maintain overall well-being. In many countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America, traditional medicine plays a significant role in meeting primary healthcare needs. For instance, in Africa, up to 80% of the population relies on traditional medicine for primary healthcare. The WHO also notes that traditional medicine is gaining popularity in industrialized nations. In the United States, for example, approximately 158 million adults use alternative medicine, which includes traditional medicine but also encompasses a broader range of practices. However, the WHO cautions that the inappropriate use of traditional medicines or practices can lead to harmful or dangerous effects. Furthermore, additional research is necessary to evaluate the efficacy and safety of many traditional practices and medicinal plants. Disciplines such as ethnomedicine, ethnobotany, and medical anthropology are central to the study of traditional medicine. Historically, early Greek scholars such as Hippocrates, Aristotle, Theophrastus, Dioscorides, and Galen were among the first to compile and document herbal knowledge. Roman writers like Pliny and Celsus also contributed to this body of knowledge. Dioscorides, for example, included the writings of Krateuas, a herbalist and physician to Mithridates VI of Pontus, in his seminal work De Materia Medica. This text was translated into multiple languages over the centuries, with additional names and annotations in Turkish, Arabic, and Hebrew. Latin manuscripts of De Materia Medica were later combined with other herbal texts, such as those by Apuleius Platonicus, and incorporated into the Anglo-Saxon codex Cotton Vitellius C III. These early Greek and Roman compilations formed the foundation of European medical theory and were subsequently translated into Arabic by scholars like Avicenna (Ibn Sīnā), Rhazes (Rāzi), and Maimonides. During the eighth and ninth centuries, Greek medical texts were translated into Arabic, which influenced the development of Arabic indigenous medicine. This system emerged from the interplay between Bedouin magic-based medicine, Hellenic medical traditions, and Ayurvedic practices. Spanish indigenous medicine, in turn, was shaped by Arabic influences during the period of Arab rule from 711 to 1492. Later, translations of these early Roman-Greek texts were made into German by Hieronymus Bock, whose herbal Kreuter Buch was published in 1546. Dutch botanist Rembert Dodoens' work Pemptades was translated into English by Henry Lyte in 1578 as A Nievve Herball, which subsequently influenced John Gerard's Herball or General Historie of Plantes. These texts were compilations of existing knowledge with new additions, and they coexisted alongside undocumented folk knowledge, particularly that of women. Many of the drugs, diluents, flavoring agents, and emollients mentioned by Dioscorides remain listed in modern European pharmacopoeias. The Puritans brought Gerard's work to the United States, where it influenced American indigenous medicine. In Mexico, Francisco Hernandez, a physician to King Philip II of Spain, documented Aztec ethnomedicinal knowledge in his work Rerum Medicarum Novae Hispaniae Thesaurus. This text, along with others like Juan de Esteyneffer's Florilegio medicinal de todas las enfermedades, incorporated European concepts of disease into indigenous knowledge. Similarly, Martin de la Cruz wrote an herbal in Nahuatl, which was translated into Latin by Juan Badiano as Libellus de medicinalibus indorum herbis and presented to King Carlos V of Spain in 1552. These works often reflected the influence of European colonization and sought to fit indigenous knowledge into European frameworks. Indigenous medicine is often transmitted orally within cultures until it is formally documented. Knowledge may be widely shared within a community or concentrated among specific healers, such as shamans or midwives. The legitimacy of a healer in indigenous medicine is based on three factors: the healer's subjective reality, the objective reality of their successful treatments, and the belief systems of the community. These belief systems, influenced by both local and global factors, impact the first two factors. Laguerre (1987) identified three types of adherents to rejected knowledge, such as indigenous medicine: permanent believers who are born and socialized into the system, temporary believers who turn to it during crises, and selective believers who accept only certain aspects of the system. Indigenous knowledge is transmitted through society and community, family, or individual experiences, such as dreams. However, elements of indigenous medicine within a culture may not form a coherent system and can sometimes be contradictory. For example, Caribbean indigenous remedies include European medicinal herbs introduced by early Spanish colonists, indigenous plants adopted from Amerindian traditions, and recently introduced ornamental plants for which curative uses have been invented without historical basis. The widespread introduction of plant species for ornamental and medicinal purposes has facilitated such inventions. Herbal medicine, a subset of indigenous medicine, involves the use of plant parts to create teas, poultices, or powders for purported therapeutic effects. In Trinidad, Spanish Catholic influences have contributed to indigenous medicine practices. For instance, it is believed that digging up fowl foot grass (Eleusine indica) on Good Friday will reveal a piece of coal beneath the roots, and cutting white or red physic nut (Jatropha curcas or Jatropha gossypifolia) on the same day will produce the blood of Jesus. Healing ceremonies, such as santowah, incorporate Spanish-Romanic prayers called oracion and the use of plants like sweet broom (Scoparia dulcis) to sprinkle holy water. Similar practices are observed in Almería, Spain. In Trinidad and Tobago, red cloths are tied around the necks of young animals to protect them from the evil eye, a practice also found in Tuscany. In the United States, indigenous medicine includes practices like apitherapy, which involves the use of bee stings or venom to treat autoimmune disorders such as arthritis and multiple sclerosis. Vermont indigenous medicine, popularized by D.C. Jarvis in his 1958 book Folk Medicine, emphasized the use of apple cider vinegar as a key ingredient in remedies. Mennonite and Amish communities brought their European indigenous medicine traditions to America in the 18th and 19th centuries, preserving their knowledge through oral traditions, farm almanacs, manuals, and handwritten recipes.
